question: The primary purpose of Software Configuration Management (SCM) is to

options.text: control and track changes to software artifacts throughout their lifecycle
execute every unit test automatically after each commit
estimate project cost from source-code size
replace requirements engineering with version labels

explanation: SCM identifies, controls, tracks, and audits changes to software artifacts so product integrity is maintained.

question: Which set of items can typically be placed under configuration management?

options.text: Source code only
Source code, requirements, design documents, test assets, build scripts, and releases
Only files that are executable after compilation
Only documents that are changed after deployment

explanation: Configuration management can cover all important artifacts, not just source code.

question: An SCM repository is best described as

options.text: a controlled store for configuration items and their history or metadata
a test environment that runs load tests
a list of defects without links to source artifacts
a temporary folder used only during compilation

explanation: A repository stores versioned configuration items and associated information such as history, branches, or metadata.

question: Which statement best distinguishes a repository from a working copy?

options.text: The repository is the managed source of stored versions; the working copy is the local copy used for editing
The working copy stores all project history while the repository stores only screenshots
They are always the same physical directory
A repository is used only for backups and cannot track versions

explanation: A working copy is the developer's checkout of files; the repository maintains managed versions and history, depending on the tool and workflow.

question: In SCM, a configuration item (CI) is

options.text: an artifact selected for configuration management
any temporary variable created while a program runs
a user who approves every pull request
a defect that has already been fixed

explanation: Configuration items are artifacts designated for identification, control, and tracking.

question: A baseline is most accurately defined as

options.text: an approved snapshot of a configuration that serves as a reference for further work
the latest unreviewed change in a developer's working directory
a list of all test failures in the current build
a branch that must be deleted after each commit

explanation: A baseline is a formally agreed configuration used as a stable reference; changes are controlled after establishment.

question: Why is a baseline useful during software development?

options.text: It provides a known reference for measuring and controlling subsequent changes
It prevents all future changes from being made
It guarantees that no defects exist in the approved version
It eliminates the need for change requests

explanation: Baselines stabilize an agreed configuration while allowing authorized, traceable changes.

question: A customer requests a change to an approved baseline. A sound SCM process should normally

options.text: evaluate, authorize, implement, and record the change through change control
modify the baseline immediately without recording it
reject every change because baselines are permanent
allow only the original author to make any future change

explanation: Controlled change management assesses impact and approval before implementing and recording a baseline change.

question: Configuration identification primarily involves

options.text: selecting and uniquely labeling configuration items and their versions
testing response time under peak load
deciding whether a feature is commercially profitable
repairing every defect found in production

explanation: Configuration identification defines the items under control and how versions and configurations are uniquely identified.

question: Configuration control primarily ensures that

options.text: changes to configuration items are evaluated and authorized before incorporation
every developer uses the same text editor
only the newest source file is retained
all test cases produce identical execution times

explanation: Configuration control governs proposed changes, approval, implementation, and traceability.

question: Configuration status accounting/reporting provides

options.text: recorded information about configuration items, versions, change requests, and their status
only a final list of unresolved compiler warnings
a guarantee that the product is secure
an automatic decision about all requested features

explanation: Status accounting records and reports the state and history of configuration items and change activity.

question: A configuration audit is mainly performed to determine whether

options.text: the product and records conform to specified configuration requirements and approved baselines
the project team has used the most popular programming language
the product contains the maximum possible number of features
the application has no performance bottlenecks whatsoever

explanation: Configuration audits check consistency between actual artifacts, documentation, and approved configuration records.

question: Which is the best example of a functional configuration audit?

options.text: Checking whether the delivered product satisfies the approved functional requirements for its baseline
Checking only whether filenames follow a naming convention
Counting commits without examining their content
Checking whether every developer has the same operating system

explanation: A Functional Configuration Audit (FCA) checks that the product's functional characteristics meet specified requirements.

question: Which is most closely associated with a Physical Configuration Audit (PCA)?

options.text: Verifying that the as-built product and its documentation correctly identify the configuration to be delivered
Testing whether all requirements are useful to customers
Measuring the average time between failures
Checking only whether each branch has a merge commit

explanation: A PCA examines the product configuration and associated documentation to establish that the released item is correctly identified and documented.

question: Version control is primarily used to

options.text: record and manage successive revisions of files and support collaboration
approve business requirements automatically
replace system testing with code history
measure reliability without operational data

explanation: Version control records revisions and helps developers compare, restore, branch, and merge changes.

question: In Git, a commit generally represents

options.text: a recorded snapshot of repository content with metadata and parent history
a temporary file that disappears after compilation
a request that has automatically been approved for production
a remote server used only for issue tracking

explanation: A Git commit records a repository snapshot and metadata such as author, message, and parent commit references.

question: Which statement about Git and SVN is generally correct?

options.text: Git is distributed, while SVN is traditionally centralized
Git is centralized, while SVN is distributed
Both require every developer to commit directly to one central server to preserve all history
Neither supports tracking file revisions

explanation: Git is a distributed version control system; Subversion (SVN) is traditionally centralized.

question: In a distributed version control system such as Git, a local clone normally contains

options.text: a local repository with project history, allowing many operations offline
only the current source files with no commit history
only the remote repository's issue list
a compiled executable but no source files

explanation: A Git clone normally contains repository data and history locally, enabling offline commits and history inspection.

question: In Git, a branch is most accurately understood as

options.text: a movable reference to a commit that supports an independent line of work
a separate physical computer for every feature
a permanent copy that cannot be merged
a file containing only the final release notes

explanation: A Git branch is a lightweight reference to a commit, commonly used to isolate work before integration.

question: A merge conflict occurs when

options.text: changes from different lines of work cannot be automatically reconciled
a commit message is longer than one line
a developer creates a branch from an older commit
a repository contains more than one file

explanation: Conflicts arise when version-control tools cannot safely combine competing edits automatically.

question: Which pairing of Git commands and common purposes is correct?

options.text: commit—record local changes; pull—fetch and integrate remote changes; push—send local commits to a remote
commit—delete history; pull—publish local commits; push—discard remote changes
commit—create a repository backup only; pull—rename a branch; push—run unit tests
commit—approve a change request; pull—create a baseline automatically; push—perform an audit

explanation: These are the common roles of commit, pull, and push in Git workflows.

question: A pull request or merge request is primarily used to

options.text: propose changes for review and controlled integration into another branch
guarantee that the proposed code contains no defects
replace the repository's version history
automatically create a software safety case

explanation: Pull/merge requests support discussion, review, checks, and approval before changes are merged.

question: A team tags a specific commit as `v2.0.0` before release. The tag primarily helps

options.text: identify an important point in repository history such as a release
automatically roll back every user's local changes
prevent all future commits to the repository
replace the release's build and test records

explanation: Tags provide stable names for significant commits, commonly release points.

question: A developer changes a tracked file locally but has not committed the change. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The working tree has modifications that are not yet recorded in a commit
The change is already part of the remote repository
The change has automatically changed the approved baseline
The change cannot be reviewed or compared

explanation: Uncommitted edits exist in the working tree and are not yet represented by a new commit.

question: Before approving a proposed change to a configuration item, the change control board should primarily review

options.text: its impact on cost, schedule, interfaces, risks, and related configuration items
only the number of lines that will be modified
whether the requester is the most senior developer
whether the change can avoid being recorded

explanation: Impact analysis evaluates technical dependencies and project consequences before a change is authorized.
